passages.t: Jehoahaz pleads, and a deliverer comes
passages.happening:
Jehoahaz son of Jehu reigns seventeen years in Samaria. He does evil and keeps the sins of Jeroboam (verses 1-2). ‘So the anger of the LORD burned against Israel’ (verse 3), and he gives them again and again into the hands of Hazael king of Aram and his son Ben-hadad.

‘Then Jehoahaz sought the favor of the LORD, and the LORD listened to him because He saw the oppression that the king of Aram had inflicted on Israel’ (verse 4). The LORD gives Israel a deliverer, and they escape Aram's power and live in their own homes again (verse 5). Yet they do not turn from the sins of Jeroboam, and the Asherah pole stays standing in Samaria (verse 6). Jehoahaz is left with only fifty horsemen, ten chariots and ten thousand foot soldiers, because the king of Aram had made the rest ‘like the dust at threshing’ (verse 7).

His son Jehoash reigns sixteen years and also does evil (verses 10-11). The narrator records his death and burial in Samaria, and his son Jeroboam takes the throne (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The story returns to the north, where Jehu's dynasty holds the throne but Jeroboam's golden calves still stand. Jehoahaz reigned about 814 to 798 BC and Jehoash, also spelled Joash, about 798 to 782 BC. Their enemy was Hazael, over whom Elisha had wept, and then his son. Aram-Damascus was at the height of its power, and Israel's tiny force shows how far it had fallen from the chariot army Ahab once led.

Verses 3 to 5 follow the pattern of the book of Judges: sin, oppression, a cry to the LORD, a deliverer, rest. The deliverer is not named. Relief came in part from outside. The Assyrian king Adad-nirari III campaigned west at the end of the ninth century and forced Damascus to pay tribute, which broke Aram's grip, and an Assyrian stela found at Tell al-Rimah in northern Iraq names Joash of Samaria among the kings who paid him tribute. Many scholars think the deliverer was Adad-nirari, serving the LORD's purpose without knowing it. Others name Jehoash, who won back the cities, or Jeroboam II, through whom 14:27 says the LORD saved Israel.

Jehoash's burial is reported before his visit to Elisha, out of order, so that the prophet's death can close the section.
passages.later: The book of Judges says that the LORD ‘was moved to pity by their groaning under those who oppressed them’ (Judges 2:18).
passages.asks: The LORD heard a king who did evil, because he saw the people's suffering. Ask whether you believe God listens even when your record is poor. And ask what it means that his people were rescued and still kept the old idols.

passages.t: Elisha's last arrow, and his bones
passages.happening:
Elisha falls sick with the illness that will kill him. King Jehoash comes down and weeps over him: “My father, my father, the chariots and horsemen of Israel!” (verse 14).

Elisha tells him to take a bow and arrows, and to put his hand on the bow, and Elisha puts his own hands on the king's hands (verses 15-16). “Open the east window,” he says (verse 17), and then tells him to shoot. ‘This is the LORD’s arrow of victory, the arrow of victory over Aram’ (verse 17), he says; the king will strike the Arameans at Aphek until they are finished. Then Elisha tells him to take the arrows and strike the ground. ‘So he struck the ground three times and stopped’ (verse 18). The man of God is angry. He should have struck five or six times and finished Aram off. ‘But now you will strike down Aram only three times’ (verse 19).

Elisha dies and is buried. Moabite raiders used to come in every spring. Once, as some Israelites are burying a man, they see a band of raiders and throw the body into Elisha's tomb. ‘And as soon as his body touched the bones of Elisha, the man was revived and stood up on his feet’ (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The long Elisha cycle that began when the cloak fell from Elijah now closes. The king's cry repeats Elisha's own words as Elijah was taken. Father was a title of honor for a prophet who led a band of disciples, and the words about chariots and horsemen named the prophet as Israel's real defense, worth more than the army Aram had destroyed.

Shooting an arrow toward enemy land seems to have served in some ancient cultures as a symbolic opening of war, and the east window looked across the Jordan toward Aram. Elisha's hands on the king's hands mark the arrow as the LORD's. Striking the ground was a sign-act, a physical action that carries out what God has said. The word for victory, teshu'ah, means rescue that comes from God.

Families used rock-cut tombs for several burials, which is how a burial party could hurry a body into a tomb already in use. Even the prophet's grave gives life. The number three runs through the ending: three strikes, and three victories.
passages.later: When Elijah was taken up, Elisha had cried, “My father, my father, the chariots and horsemen of Israel!” (2 Kings 2:12). The same words are now said over him. Elijah and Elisha had each raised a dead son in their lifetimes (1 Kings 17:17-24; 2 Kings 4:32-37), and Hebrews remembers that ‘Women received back their dead, raised to life again’ (Hebrews 11:35).
passages.hard:
Is the story of Elisha's bones a kind of magic, and why was Elisha angry at a king who did what he was told?

The revival in verse 21 is told briefly and without comment. Some readers have taken it as support for honoring the remains of holy people, a practice with a long history in parts of the church. Others note that no one in the story seeks out the bones, prays to Elisha or keeps them as a relic. The man was thrown in by frightened mourners, and the power belongs to the LORD, who shows that the word Elisha spoke is still alive after his death. Either way, the story does not make the bones a tool people can use.

Elisha's anger can seem unfair, since he never told the king how many times to strike. But the sign-act tested what the king expected. Jehoash had just heard that the LORD would give victory over Aram until it was finished. Striking three times and stopping showed a man who wanted a little relief rather than the full rescue promised. The fault lay not in failing to guess a number but in the smallness of his hope.
passages.asks: Jehoash struck the ground three times and stopped. Ask where you have settled for less than God has offered. And ask whom you have honored with tears while refusing to change what they called you to change.

passages.t: For the sake of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
passages.happening:
Hazael oppresses Israel all through the reign of Jehoahaz (verse 22). ‘But the LORD was gracious to Israel and had compassion on them, and He turned toward them because of His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. And to this day, the LORD has been unwilling to destroy them or cast them from His presence’ (verse 23).

Hazael dies, and his son Ben-hadad reigns (verse 24). Jehoash takes back from him the cities Hazael had taken from his father. He defeats Ben-hadad three times and recovers the cities of Israel (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
Verse 23 stands at the center of the ending as the narrator's explanation of everything around it. Israel survives not because it repented, which the chapter plainly says it did not, but because of God's covenant with the patriarchs, older than the kingdom and older than the law at Sinai. The verb for compassion, racham, is related to the Hebrew word for womb, and it describes the tender pity of a parent for a child.

This mercy sets up the recovery under Jeroboam II in the next chapter. It also makes the final fall of Samaria in chapter 17 more sobering, since the words to this day point to a patience that would one day end. The three victories match the three strikes of the arrows.
passages.later: In Egypt too, ‘God heard their groaning, and He remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob’ (Exodus 2:24). A psalm says, ‘As a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear Him’ (Psalm 103:13). Zechariah praised God ‘to show mercy to our fathers and to remember His holy covenant’ (Luke 1:72).
passages.asks: Israel was held by God's promise, not by its own faithfulness. Ask how that shapes the way you think about God's patience with you. And ask whether you have treated that patience as permission or as a door left open.
